razonamiento:
I'm thinking through concepts for a creature that's geometrically or biologically impossible—maybe combining a Penrose-triangle body with mismatched animal features, or contradictory traits like a fish with lungs walking on land. I want something genuinely creative and visually fun to render in SVG.

Calculating Penrose triangle coordinates...

I'm working out the geometry by constructing the tribar from three identical elbow-shaped hexagons rotated 120° apart around the center, defining outer triangle vertices and a smaller scaled inner hole triangle to form each piece's shape.

I'm trying to set up an isometric grid with three axis directions at 120° apart to construct the tribar's beams, thinking through how each beam's outline traces the overall triangular shape.

Actually, recalling the image more carefully — the outer silhouette isn't a clean triangle but has each corner truncated, showing the square end-face of a beam where it terminates.

All three outer corners come to sharp points, so I should work this out more rigorously using a 3D construction with three bars along orthogonal axes, projecting each cuboid into 2D to figure out exactly where the cut faces and overlaps fall.

Actually this geometric reconstruction is taking too long — let me abandon the Penrose triangle approach entirely and pivot to something simpler: a chimera-style creature, since the task is just to depict "an animal that cannot exist," which a hybrid creature satisfies just as well as a literal impossible object.

I decide the Penrose triangle is worth doing properly, so I work out isometric coordinates for it — setting up three beams extending along each axis from a shared corner cube, forming a tripod shape that creates the classic impossible-triangle illusion when rendered.

Recalling the well-known Wikipedia SVG path data for the Penrose triangle, I start reconstructing its path coordinates for the drawing.

I'm reconsidering the geometry: the inner hole should be a concentric equilateral triangle with the same orientation as the outer one, with three bars forming the classic elbow shapes and joint lines at each corner. I'll build this as three congruent hexagonal "elbow" pieces defining the bars between outer and inner edges.

Working out beam coordinates in 3D...

I'm defining the three rectangular beams along the X, Y, and Z axes with unit cross-sections, sharing a common unit cube at the corner, then projecting them isometrically to check whether the far end of one beam visually lines up with another beam's end to create the Penrose triangle illusion.

Computing the projected positions, I find the three arm-ends actually form a symmetric equilateral triangle rather than coinciding directly — so the illusion must work by joining adjacent arm-ends in 2D, which is impossible in true 3D but reads as a continuous loop in projection.

I reconsider the construction: the real tribar isn't three beams radiating from a center, but three separate beams each forming one side of the triangle, connected end-to-end like a staircase — beam one running along X from corner A to B, beam two along Z, and so on.

I'm checking whether this staircase of beams closes up correctly when projected into 2D, computing each corner's position to see if the projected shape actually forms a closed triangle even though the 3D path doesn't connect back to its start.

Good, the triangle checks out with side length L. Now I need to build actual 3D beams of width w along this triangular centerline, so I'll set up coordinate ranges for each beam's cross-section, starting with beam A along the X-axis with defined y and z extents, then handle proper occlusion where beams meet at the joints.

I can draw them joined visually, hiding that discontinuity. Now I'm setting up the projection formula for isometric view, with L=100 and w=30 for the beam dimensions, and working out which faces of beam A are visible from the viewer's angle at (+∞,+∞,+∞) — likely the top face and the two faces facing the viewer.

Computing the projected coordinates of beam A's box corners...

I'm noting that the silhouette of an axis-aligned box in isometric view forms a hexagon that excludes the nearest and farthest corners, and I'm working out which vertices define that hexagon's boundary.

I'm listing the six projected coordinates in order: (-25.98,15), (-25.98,-15), (0,-30), (86.6,20), (86.6,50), (60.62,65), then closing back to the first point to complete the loop.

I confirm the hexagon is convex by checking that all the turns go the same direction. Now I'm identifying which faces of beam A are visible, starting with the top face (z=30) and the y=30 side face, projecting their four corners each into the 2D coordinates already computed.

Given the complexity of this full 3D computation across three beams, I'm reconsidering whether to actually fully render the Penrose triangle geometry with occlusion, or to simplify by drawing the classic flat outline with an outer triangle, inner triangular hole, and a few internal division lines to suggest the beams. I'm also weighing whether to abandon the Penrose triangle idea altogether in favor of a simpler impossible object, like a hybrid creature with a knotted or impossible neck.

Actually, I like the idea of using the "devil's fork" illusion instead — a creature whose three cylindrical legs merge into two rectangular legs at the top, since that's much easier to draw convincingly while still being unmistakably impossible. I'll sketch a quadruped-like body standing on this impossible trident, possibly adding extra strange features for flair.

Working out the blivet's geometry now...

I'm picturing the classic blivet orientation flipped vertically: a solid rectangular block at top with two bars (110-150 and 190-230) and a gap between them, from which three cylindrical prongs appear to emerge below, creating the impossible-object illusion through ambiguous edge connections.

I'm working through the illusion mechanics now, figuring out how the two visible bars at the top should only show two prongs while the ambiguous middle cylinder emerges from the gap between them, tracing where the outer silhouette edges need to connect for the impossible trident effect to read correctly.

I'm realizing the real trick: the four long lines defining the two bars (edges a, b, c, d) actually double as the edges of three cylinders on the prong side — the gap between the bars becomes one of the prong bodies itself, not a separate shape.

I'm trying to settle the actual line count: three cylinders on the prong side with two edges each would be six lines, while the bar side has two bars with two edges each for four lines, but some lines must terminate at the transition zone rather than running the full length. I think the cleanest approach is to just sketch out the shape directly rather than keep reasoning abstractly about line counts.

I'm working out the coordinates for the left and right bars, the slot between them that stays open toward the prong side but closes higher up, and the three prongs extending from those bars plus a middle prong in between.

This gives me exactly the blivet illusion: three cylindrical prongs below merging into two rectangular bars with a slot above. I'm adjusting the middle prong's width slightly and how its edges meet the tips of the outer prongs to make the impossible gap read convincingly.

I'm reconsidering the middle prong's edges — for the illusion to work properly, they need to visually connect to the bars' inner edges (x=145 and 195) rather than floating independently, since that shared-edge ambiguity is what makes the blivet impossible rather than just look like a careless sketch.

Now I'm building out the creature on top of this impossible leg structure: a body/rump blob merging into the block, a neck and head to the upper left, maybe a beak or antlers for extra strangeness, and possibly eye stalks. I want to keep the overall design elegant, with the impossible legs as the core illusion rather than piling on too many extra tricks.

I'm planning the full composition now — a curved neck rising to a head with snout, eye, and ears, plus a tail curving off the other side that could end in a second small head for an extra twist. I'll use a lavender/teal palette against a warm background, then start writing the SVG: background gradient, shadow ellipse, tail behind the body, and the legs group drawn first so the body layers over them.

Now I'm working out how the body blob's flat bottom should sit over the bars so they read as flush rectangular attachments, with the gap between bars left unfilled so it shows the background color as a slot, and the prongs continuing seamlessly from the bars as one shape.

Each prong needs a rounded capsule tip rather than a flat bottom, so I'm switching to a path with a straight section down to near the bottom then a semicircular arc for the tip, sized to the 45px prong width. I'm also adding a horizontal gradient to give the prongs cylindrical shading so they read as rounded rather than flat.

Actually, thinking about the classic blivet illusion more, it works purely through line art without shading at all—the flat bars read as flat because the closed slot line implies it, so I might skip gradients entirely and rely on clean outlines for the ambiguity to land.

Writing the prong path coordinates...

I'm tracing through the arc direction using clock positions — checking whether going from the 9 o'clock point through 6 o'clock to 3 o'clock reads as clockwise or counterclockwise on screen, to get the sweep-flag right for the rounded bottom.

Now I'm sketching out the paths for the middle and right prongs, working out their x-coordinates and widths so the gaps between them line up consistently.

Finishing the right bar path, then checking that the slot region between the left and right bars stays as background since only the two bars get drawn there. I'm considering adding a subtle arc or line at the slot's closed end so it reads clearly as a rounded slot rather than an open gap.

Now I'm shaping the body as a plump rounded form sitting atop the bars, using curved path segments to give it a back and belly, with the bottom edge implicitly closing against the bars. Next I'm working out the neck and head — a curve rising from the upper body to a head positioned above, with a long snout shape to suggest the creature's profile.

I'm deciding on the overall creature design: a blob-like body with legs, a long curling neck ending in a big-eyed head with small horns, and a tail that curls up into a second smaller head facing the first — skipping the wing idea in favor of dorsal spikes for a cleaner silhouette. Now I'm settling on a color palette, pairing a soft cream background gradient with a teal body tone and dark outlines.

Writing the neck and head paths...

Still writing tail shape... I'll finish it with a small secondary head at the tip, add triangular fin spikes along the back, and drop in a soft ground shadow ellipse beneath the creature for depth, plus curling antennae stalks from the head.

Adding a small wing detail on the back for extra charm, then I'm sequencing the draw order—background, shadow, tail, neck, legs, then body layered on top so the leg-body seams stay hidden.

I realize the straight body-bottom edge would cut across the leg bars, so instead I'm merging the body and both legs into a single continuous outline path with a notch for the gap, letting the bars flow naturally into the body shape.

Still tracing the outline path...

Finishing the back curve of the body outline, then realizing the middle prong should be drawn as an open path without a closing "Z" so the stroke doesn't draw a top line, letting the fill close the shape implicitly for that classic blivet look.

I'll order the drawing so the neck sits behind the body and the head is drawn after, with the neck emerging from the body's top-left and curving upward to meet the head, then shaping the head as a rounded blob overlapping the neck's top.

Now I'm adding a small pointed beak on the left side, a round white eye with a dark pupil and tiny highlight, plus two curved antennae stalks each ending in a small circle. I'm also starting the tail, which curves out from the body and back toward a second head shape, drawn behind the main body so it reads as if it's emerging from underneath.

Writing SVG code...

Adding dorsal spike triangles behind the body, drawn first in the group so they read as fins peeking above the back curve, with a slightly darker fill for contrast.

respuesta: Dibujé una criatura imposible: un bicho rechoncho, azul pálido, parado sobre unas patas que son un truco óptico —si las seguís con la vista, nunca terminás de contar cuántas son; los contornos se cruzan y se cancelan solos—. Tiene una sola ala, chica e inútil, en el medio del lomo; tres aletas dorsales como de pez; dos antenitas con pelotitas rosadas; y una cola gruesa que se curva hacia arriba y termina en una segunda cabeza con su propio pico y su propio ojo, mirando para el otro lado. Ambas cabezas parecen tranquilas, como si esta anatomía fuera lo más normal del mundo.
